newsitem.title: BELGIUM: MEPs in bid to speed up gas liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: MEPs in bid to speed up gas liberalisation.

text.p: The European Parliament is expected to attempt on November 12 to speed up the liberalisation of the European Union gas sector.
The move comes less than a month before EU energy ministers and Euro-MPs are due to approve a draft directive which will partially open up the EU electricity market to competition.

Although the controversial electricity directive does not go far enough to satisfy liberalisation-minded member states and Euro-MPs, which include the largely Christian Democrat European People's Party (EPP), the majority view is that it is at least a first step in the right direction.

In an attempt to ensure a forthcoming sister directive on the gas market introduces a greater degree of liberalisation, Dutch EPP member Wim van Velzen plans to send a string of recommendations to the European Commission and the Council ahead of the Council's first debate on the directive on December 3.
The recommendations are contained in a report on the Commission's white paper on EU energy policy -- COM(95)682 -- which parliament is expected to approve next Tuesday.
They include statements on introducing competition in the gas distribution sector and the need for EU dispute settlement procedures.
These were two of the most controversial elements in the long, drawn-out debate on electricity liberalisation and were left out of the final text of the directive.

"I'm very happy to notice the Irish Presidency has included a lot of those elements in the draft gas directive," Van Velzen told Reuters, adding that Energy Commissioner Christos Papoutsis also seemed enthusiastic.
Van Velzen said he was generally satisfied with the white paper, which takes up most of the recommendations Parliament made on the Commission's energy green paper in October 1995.

However, the Dutch Euro-MP's report on the white paper urges the Commission to commit itself to a larger number of specific policy initiatives, including action to increase the percentage of renewable energy sources in the EU's energy mix.

"The white paper includes a programme of Commission activities for the next two to three years. We are a bit negative about the Commission's ambition. They are not doing enough. We want more action," Van Velzen explained.
He said the Commission had already reacted to some of the draft report's calls for swifter, practical action.
"There will be communications on renewable energy and cogeneration very soon. They will be dealt with during the Dutch Presidency (of the Council in 1997).
"There is also the gas directive: there will be a first draft by December 3 and we expect it will be finalised during the Dutch Presidency," he said.

Like the green paper before it, the white paper put too much emphasis on the need to make European industry more competitive and too little on protecting the environment, and Parliament should seek to redress the balance, Van Velzen said.

He added that the current Irish Presidency and the Dutch, who take over from Dublin in January, both welcomed his call for more concrete measures to increase energy efficiency and energy saving, introduce higher taxes on pollutant energy resources and put more money into making Eastern Europe's nuclear plants safer.
Parliament's energy committee approved Van Velzen's report by a large majority. The rapporteur said he expected to win a similar degree of support when the full Parliament votes next Tuesday.
